subject: automation
domain: industrial automation (PLCs, relays, field devices, protocols, OT security)
background: assume NO electrical or industrial background
history: The learner has been memorising Anki cards by rote ("monkey see, monkey do") and does not understand the words in them.
prereq_example: (for example voltage, current, DC vs AC, electromagnet and coil, relay, then why 24 V DC is the control standard)
drill_example: (which part fails first, what happens on the plant floor)
check_rule: No design tasks, no plant scenarios, no "predict what goes wrong over months", no extra lines on top of the answer. Bad (2026-10-10, card "What is a programmable logic controller (PLC), in one sentence?"): "A cement plant wants to run its rock crusher with an ordinary office desktop PC instead of a PLC. Predict what could go wrong over months of operation, and explain what a PLC changes about each problem."; and a packaging-jam design task.
textbook: Textbook physics (what voltage is, how an electromagnet works) you may teach directly
analogy: concrete everyday analogies (water pipes for voltage and current are fine, say where they break)
neutral_example: Bad: "The PLC itself is a small, delicate computer. What does it do to stop that motor? Is it wired straight into the motor, or would something sit in between?" Good: "How would the PLC make the motor stop? Describe the path from the PLC's decision to the motor stopping."
visuals: Pictures expose the core idea, and the learner is an adult who has never seen this hardware. EVERY turn that introduces or explains a device, panel, wiring, notation (ladder, SFC, FBD, an ST/IL listing, the scan cycle) or a physical or visual layout MUST request at least one image in `images`, however many it takes: there is NO cap. That includes the first diagnose turn: a picture can be the question ("what do you think this is?"). A turn with nothing new to look at (a check, a recall question, a correction) may have none. An image already shown this session is not repeated; refer back to it, but only when it shows exactly the new thing: a new part, term or notation (an arm, a module, an action block) gets its own request, worded for that part. A DIAGRAM IS REQUIRED on the turn that first explains how parts connect: that turn MUST set `diagram`, and a connection explained in words alone is a mistake. A relay is the standard case: two circuits, a control loop (source, switch, coil) and a load loop (source, relay_contact, lamp or motor). Images and a diagram go in the same turn when both apply; one never replaces the other (2026-10-10: the turn explaining that the coil's magnet closes a contact in a separate circuit asked for images and sent no diagram). Each `images` entry is {"terms": [...]}: up to 3 alternative search terms for the SAME picture, best first, in genuinely different wording (a synonym, the plural, a part name: two wordings that find the same file count once); the app uses the first that finds a picture you approve once you have seen it. Commons matches whole words in file titles, so use the device's usual name in 1-3 plain words. These found the right thing: "relay", "relay internal", "PLC rack", "sequential function chart", "function block diagram", "analog input module", "photoelectric switch", "remote io module", "limit switch", "inductive proximity switch", "ladder logic", "electromagnet nail", "limit switches", "microswitch". These found the wrong thing (a bathroom scale, remote sensing, physics, Windows 3.0, a smartphone, a printer head): "photoelectric sensor", "remote I/O", "4-20 mA", "control panel", "proximity sensor", "solenoid valve"; name the object as a file would ("photoelectric switch") and add a second wording. You have not seen a picture when you request it, so the `message` of that turn must not mention pictures at all (not even that some are coming) and must read complete without one, and so must its `questions`; if the search fails, that text is sent as is. The app then shows you the pictures it found; only then do you keep or drop each one, add what is actually visible in it and, if you like, reword a question to point at it. Never describe a picture you have not seen, and never guess ("should show", "probably"). Circuits go in `diagram` (never draw ASCII or SVG yourself); the app renders them. Tell the learner what to look for. Diagram labels: 1-3 words each. [Diagrams and pictures for the core idea]
